paragraphs.heading: A warm, fast current
paragraphs.text: The Gulf Stream is a warm, quick current in the Atlantic Ocean. It starts in the Gulf of Mexico, passes through the Straits of Florida and runs up the east coast of the United States. Near 36°N, off North Carolina, it turns east and heads toward Northwest Europe as the North Atlantic Current. Around 40°N 30°W it splits: the North Atlantic Drift goes on to Northern Europe, while the Canary Current loops back past West Africa.

paragraphs.heading: Why the west side is strong
paragraphs.text: The Gulf Stream is mostly driven by the push of the wind on the sea. In the tropics the trade winds blow west, and at mid-latitudes the westerlies blow east. A process called western intensification then makes currents on the western edge of an ocean basin, like the Gulf Stream, stronger than those on the eastern edge. The current also bends as it flows, and these bends sometimes break off to form separate warm and cold eddies.

paragraphs.heading: Size and speed
paragraphs.text: Through the Florida Straits the Gulf Stream carries 30 million cubic metres of water a second, or 30 sverdrups. South of Newfoundland that grows to 150 sverdrups. All the rivers that flow into the Atlantic together add up to only 0.6 sverdrups, though the Antarctic Circumpolar Current is stronger still. The stream is usually about 100 km wide and 800 to 1,200 m deep, and it moves fastest at the top, at up to about 2.5 m/s. It sits closer to the North American coast in summer and further out in winter.

paragraphs.heading: Shaping climate on both shores
paragraphs.text: The Gulf Stream affects the climate of the US East Coast from Florida to southeast Virginia, and Northwest Europe even more. There is a consensus that Northwest Europe is warmer than other places at similar latitudes at least partly because of the strong North Atlantic Current. That current, mostly driven by the thermohaline circulation, carries warm water northeast, making Western and especially Northern Europe milder. The Gulf Stream has also helped strong cyclones of every kind develop, in the air and in the sea.

paragraphs.heading: Franklin's chart
paragraphs.text: Europeans learned of the Gulf Stream on Juan Ponce de León's expedition in 1512, after which Spanish ships sailing from the Caribbean to Spain used it widely. Later Benjamin Franklin asked his cousin Timothy Folger, a whaling captain from Nantucket, about it. Folger said merchant ships routinely crossed the current, spotting it by whales, water temperature and colour, while mail ship captains sailed against it. Folger drew its path on a chart of the Atlantic, which was printed in London in 1769 but mostly ignored by British captains.

paragraphs.heading: Watching from space
paragraphs.text: Direct measurements of the current's speed and temperature began in the 1950s and 1960s, using research ships and current meters anchored in place. From the late 1970s, satellites measuring surface temperature, sea height and ocean colour let scientists map where the current is in close to real time. NASA's TOPEX/Poseidon mission, launched in 1992, and the missions after it kept a steady record of sea-surface height. Drifting buoys and Argo floats now also measure temperature and salt below the surface, giving a three-dimensional picture of the current.
